items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

About 20 Indigenous Awá living in isolation approached the Guajajara village of Tawari on Monday, November 16, in Arariboia Indigenous Territory, in the Brazilian state of Maranhão; they received yams and returned to the forest. Members of the Guajajara community recorded the encounter, and the organization Survival International shared the footage. The National Foundation for Indigenous Peoples (Funai) and Indigenous health personnel are in the area. The government activated an emergency coordination mechanism to assess the situation and health risks. Authorities said they are still assessing the initial information and that this isolated approach does not mean the Awá have abandoned their isolation. The reason for the visit has not been confirmed; Survival International linked it to pressure from illegal loggers, hunters, and ranchers on the territory. Local residents voiced concern about the thinness of some children and older people. There is also concern about the risk of infections, given the group’s limited exposure to common pathogens.

items.title: [phys.org] COP31 nations split over 1.5°C goal as threshold nears
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Halfway through the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, countries are divided over whether to keep the 1.5°C warming limit as a central goal after the United Nations said in September that crossing it was imminent and unavoidable. Global temperatures have risen about 1.4°C above pre-industrial levels. Some countries want the summit’s final decision to reaffirm 1.5°C as the “right goal” and call for temperatures to return below that limit as soon as possible. Other negotiators, including members of the Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, are pushing to weaken or remove references to the target. Scientists say reversing an overshoot would require sharp emissions cuts and large-scale carbon removal over decades; University of Exeter climate scientist Pierre Friedlingstein described that prospect as “extremely ambitious”.

Forty large pension funds, insurers and sovereign wealth funds warned at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya that climate impacts threaten financial stability. Investors at a closed-door meeting said climate finance needs private capital, but some asset owners remain cautious about emerging-market projects because they lack reliable ways to assess and manage the risks. Developing countries including India are pressing for clearer obligations and more adaptation funding, while the European Union favors using existing finance mechanisms rather than creating a new work program. Outside the talks, organizers said more than 10,000 people joined a Nov. 14 climate march calling for grants, support for affected communities and a transition away from fossil fuels. Negotiators have a 104-paragraph climate-finance draft, released Nov. 14, and are due to continue discussions on finance and a just transition in the summit’s second week.

Amy Pope, director general of the International Organization for Migration (IOM), warned at the United Nations climate conference, COP31, in Antalya, Turkey, that more than 200 million people living in highly climate-vulnerable communities are at risk of displacement. IOM data show storms, drought, wildfires, extreme temperatures and floods forced nearly 30 million people from their homes in 2025. Pope said governments spend billions of dollars on border security while underfunding adaptation measures that could help communities remain in place. She estimated the cost of those measures at about $310 billion, compared with roughly $30 billion in funding so far. She argued that helping communities adapt before displacement occurs is more humane and cost-effective than responding to irregular migration after it begins.

🌲 ✏️

Investigators have linked the communications overload behind Friday’s nationwide U.S. flight halt to a recently installed router at a Federal Aviation Administration radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, according to a Wall Street Journal investigation. A radar installation in Amarillo, Texas, also generated abnormal traffic. The disruption affected 17 of the FAA’s 22 en-route centers after initial communication glitches appeared at its Indianapolis center. Officials are examining whether the fault involved defective equipment, installation or configuration. They said the system stabilized after the Arkansas and Texas devices were disconnected and a router-broadcast feature was disabled across the FAA’s roughly 60 Juniper routers. Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns Juniper Networks, said its devices operated as intended. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said investigators had not determined the cause. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford predicted that airlines would largely restore schedules by late Sunday, Nov. 15; more than 530 Sunday flights had already been canceled by Saturday evening.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

The latest report on the magnitude 6.7 earthquake that struck central Peru on Friday put the toll at one dead, 16 injured, 853 people left homeless and another 529 affected. The deceased was a 45-year-old man who had been admitted to Hermilio Valdizán Medrano Regional Hospital in Huánuco; authorities did not specify the cause of his death. The report counted 152 uninhabitable homes and 156 damaged ones, as well as damage to six schools, 22 health facilities, four churches, three community centers and about 300 meters of roads. Huánuco, Pasco and Junín sustained the most damage; Lima and Callao were also affected. Authorities deployed medical personnel, ambulances, emergency response teams and technical crews, and coordinated humanitarian aid with local governments. In Huánuco, they sent machinery to clear roads blocked by rocks. Damage assessments and repairs to restore electricity are ongoing. The Geophysical Institute of Peru reported two subsequent earthquakes in Junín, with no new damage confirmed.

items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Lightning struck NASA’s Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket twice within seconds of its Nov. 14, 1969, launch, disrupting spacecraft telemetry and endangering the mission. Mission Control engineer John Aaron recognized the readings from an earlier test and recommended switching the Signal Conditioning Equipment to its auxiliary setting, which restored the data. Investigators concluded the rocket and its conductive exhaust plume had triggered a discharge in an electrically charged part of the atmosphere, even though no active thunderstorm lay along the immediate flight path. NASA expanded launch weather restrictions to account for atmospheric electrical conditions, not only visible lightning and thunderstorms.

items.content_html:

MIT researchers found that older adults had significantly weaker waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which helps clear waste from the brain during sleep, than younger adults. The researchers used brain imaging and electroencephalography to study volunteers ages 18 to 39 and 60 to 84, linking the reduced flow partly to weaker deep-sleep brain waves and diminished vascular responses. Separately, a study described in a paper shared on Reddit found that LSD-related gene-expression patterns in rats and mice ran counter to some patterns associated with human brain aging. LSD also reduced certain amyloid-beta-related changes in mouse brain-cell cultures. These are preclinical findings, not evidence that LSD prevents dementia in people.

items.title: [Fast Company] CrowdStrike CEO: Companies are choosing between getting hacked and shutting down
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Microsoft systems down. Air traffic systems down. Problems at Chase, United, and Apple. After a week of outages across big systems, the AI conspiracy theories are in full swing. CrowdStrike founder and CEO George Kurtz describes how AI agents can turn a patch into a working exploit within an hour, and how CEOs are now taking services offline rather than risk being hacked. He also discusses CrowdStrike’s new AI Kill Switch, and why slowing down the frontier labs won’t slow down the attackers.

This is an abridged transcript of an interview from Rapid Response, hosted by former Fast Company editor-in-chief Robert Safian. From the team behind the Masters of Scale podcast, Rapid Response features candid conversations with today’s top business leaders navigating real-time challenges. Subscribe to Rapid Response wherever you get your podcasts to ensure you never miss an episode.

So what is going on? Over the past week, we’ve seen Microsoft systems go down. Air traffic systems go down. . . . The AI conspiracy theories are everywhere. Is all this just a coincidence?

I think a few of my friends and colleagues might have their tinfoil hats on as well. The reality is it’s the bill for the Mythos moment. Nine months ago, when Mythos came out, it really set in motion everyone looking for these vulnerabilities, right? And the whole industry has been racing to find as many vulnerabilities as it can and create as many patches as it can. But what we’ve done now is hit the sound barrier of actually being able to roll out all these patches. So when you look at what’s really taking place, and you look at all the issues that were found in Black October, you’ve got Darker November.

This is like the PHP code, and now Java, that people are scrambling to find and plug these gaps in.

Yeah, exactly. I think the Java one is actually going to be worse. There are already working exploits for all of that. But what people are doing now is rushing to roll out all of these patches, and they’re making the decision: Breach or break. That is, are we going to get breached because we can’t patch fast enough, or are we just going to break something and hopefully fix it if we roll it out? That’s kind of a new norm now because the industry can’t keep up.

Technology is messy. Things happen, and we’re going to get better and better as an industry at dealing with this sort of AI speed that we’re facing. When you think about all the legacy systems that are out there, and you think about even banking-type systems, there’s a lot of legacy-type code out there, and it’s not as easy just to create a fix while everything is in midstream. So it’s not always clear, and when things are melting down, you get on these 24-hour bridges, and people are trying to figure out what actually happened. It’s a bit of fog of war.

As you describe it and go through these examples, the air traffic one seems like a particularly fragile one. Is the system fragile?

I think technology is just fragile, whether you’re in an Apple ecosystem, Android, or you use Microsoft or Google, whatever you’re using. Every day people use this, and they sort of just expect it to work, and they should. But behind the scenes, when you actually look at how complicated these systems are, how they operate, and the interaction with hardware and software, disks get full, memory gets overloaded. You would think that all this has been worked out, but there’s a lot of just making stuff work in the background. And the technology folks, the men and women who have to keep this running, literally wake up every day and are just like, “OK, what are we going to have to deal with today?”

We’ve had other kinds of cyber troubles recently: OpenAI’s agents breaking into Hugging Face, and French supermarkets hit by hackers shutting down refrigeration systems, which seem like a different order of things. Are any of these episodes an “aha” moment for you, of us sort of crossing a threshold?

When you look at the latest Patch Tuesday from Microsoft, it was 1,000-plus vulnerabilities that were fixed. And again, this has spiked. . . . I think we’ve had 25% of all the vulnerabilities ever created found in the last year. Just to give you an idea of the order of magnitude of what we have to deal with.

So all these patches come out, and now what we’re seeing is the automation by AI agents and threat actors, where they will take a patch and compare what was patched versus what wasn’t patched, and they immediately know where the flaw was. Then they automate the vulnerability exploitation of that. Within an hour, you can have all that done, where that would take a nation-state actor maybe weeks to do.

So the fact that we’re starting to see these issues come up as quickly as we are, I’m not surprised. But when you think about the refrigeration systems, this was a big one in Europe. What does AI allow you to do? There’s probably a handful of people, relatively speaking, on planet Earth who understand how to program these refrigeration systems. But when you actually take an AI agent and go, “Hey, I don’t know much about the refrigeration system. You figure out how to program it,” it will figure that out. You don’t have to be an expert in any of these technologies now. And typically they’re underprotected because it’s a refrigerator. Nobody really thought about security when they were building it.

How much of the game is becoming like “My AI is better than their AI?” You have to stay ahead of the attacks.

It’s the old Spy vs. Spy cartoon. It’s really what it is, right? Who’s going to stay ahead?

You recently launched a product called the AI Kill Switch. Which is designed to stop rogue agents. How do you know which scenarios would prompt hitting the kill switch?

If you think about industry, if there was a manufacturing problem with a big machine, there’s always the red button. It’s like, stop that thing because it could be causing bodily harm. And it’s the same scenario. Are the agents doing something they shouldn’t be doing? Are they multiplying, attacking other systems, or bringing down systems internally? You want to be able to hit the button. The challenge with the kill switch is there’s blunt force. It’s almost like pulling the plug.

You work closely with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Dario Amodei at Anthropic has called on the industry to slow down. There’s been quite a lot of noise about it, although development keeps steaming ahead. Do you give OpenAI and Anthropic advice about speeding versus slowing?

At the end of the day, the genie is out of the bottle. You can slow whatever you want down on the frontier. The open-weight models are three months behind. Just slowing them down is not going to slow the rest of the world down. But keep in mind, and I just want to make this distinction, Bob, they are called labs. Okay, labs. What happens in a lab? You develop something, it kind of works, it does great things, but when you put it in the real world, it may not actually work as intended in the lab, which is why the security industry has now moved into the safety industry and has become a great opportunity for folks like us.

Anyone can slow down. If the model is not right, if it’s not aligned, if it’s not getting the output you want, if the quality control is not there, you know what you do? You don’t release it. You go back and do another run until you get it right.

So what should any business leader do right now to improve their cyber footing?

Well, I think maybe first is go find your security and IT people and give them a hug, because they are at 110% of capacity now. I’ve never seen this before, but it’s happening across industry. Company CEOs are making a decision: Take something offline or be hacked. They’re saying, “Hey, we would rather take a massive service offline than be hacked.” They’re willing to make that decision if it’s so bad. When PHP came out, I had plenty of companies say, “Hey, we may just take everything down because it’s so bad.”

European Council President António Costa’s revised 2028-34 budget proposal would cut EU cohesion funding for the first time, reducing regional development funding by €8 billion compared with the Irish presidency’s previous draft. The change affects a coalition of 17 southern and eastern member states, including Poland, Italy and Spain, that had opposed cuts to cohesion funding. Costa’s proposal also reduces allocations for competitiveness, defence and external action. It leaves direct farm subsidies unchanged from the previous draft, but France says the proposed Common Agricultural Policy funding still fails to guarantee farmers’ income support. The revised framework cuts €204 billion from the European Commission’s original plan. EU leaders will discuss the proposal at a special summit in Brussels on November 26-27. The European Parliament must also approve the eventual budget, and its chief budget negotiator, Siegfried Muresan, has warned that lawmakers may withhold consent over the reductions.

items.title: [cbc.ca] B.C. tribunal overturns $100,000 fine against X over intimate image
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

British Columbia’s Civil Resolution Tribunal has overturned a $100,000 penalty against social media platform X for failing to delete an intimate image posted without a woman’s consent, ruling that blocking access to it in Canada was a reasonable step under provincial law. The tribunal said the law did not make X liable after it blocked Canadian access to the image, which remained available outside Canada. The decision reversed a September 2025 penalty for failing to comply with an order to delete it. The tribunal accepted X’s argument that requiring worldwide removal could interfere with other countries’ legal systems and cited a 2024 Australian case as persuasive but not binding. Outgoing B.C. Attorney General Niki Sharma criticized X’s refusal to remove the image and said governments may need to strengthen laws or pursue legal action. The tribunal also rejected X’s request to require the complainant to pay more than US$100,000 in legal fees.

items.title: [aawsat.com] Jaramana car bombing prompts searches in Druze-majority Damascus suburb
items.content_html:
🌲 ✏️

Security teams in Jaramana searched vehicles and checked surveillance cameras after a car bomb struck a residential area near al-Naseem garage, damaging nearby cars and buildings, according to reports. The blast on Saturday, Nov. 14, killed a man and a girl, according to medical sources cited by Asharq Al-Awsat and Al Jazeera. Reports differed on the number of wounded: Syria’s state television said two people were wounded, while the Interior Ministry reported one. The explosion occurred near a battery-production site in Jaramana, a Damascus suburb with a large Druze community. Syria’s Internal Security Forces cordoned off the area and opened an investigation. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights said accounts differed over the blast’s precise location and nature, and verification was continuing. Residents told Asharq Al-Awsat they heard the blast at about 8 p.m. and saw the car burning. Security vehicles arrived within minutes, and streets leading to the site were closed, with access allowed for ambulances and civil defense crews.
